```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
library(data.table)
library(here)

# Load scalars produced by estimation scripts.
# Run order: estimate-sumstats-nfip.R, estimate-mhs.R, estimate-nfip.R,
#            then estimate-welfare.R (depends on the other two).
mhs_sc  <- fread(here("output", "results", "mhs-scalars.csv"))
nfip_sc <- fread(here("output", "results", "nfip-scalars.csv"))
welf_sc <- fread(here("output", "results", "welfare-scalars.csv"))
ss_sc   <- fread(here("output", "results", "sumstats-nfip-scalars.csv"))

get_mhs  <- function(nm) mhs_sc[statistic == nm,  value]
get_nfip <- function(nm) nfip_sc[statistic == nm, value]
get_welf <- function(nm) welf_sc[statistic == nm, value]
get_ss   <- function(nm) ss_sc[statistic == nm,   value]

# Formatting helpers.  All monetary values stored in $000 (2000 dollars).
fmt_d <- function(x, digits = 0) {
    paste0("\\$", formatC(abs(round(x * 1000)), format = "f",
                          digits = digits, big.mark = ","))
}
fmt_pct <- function(x, digits = 0) {
    paste0(formatC(round(x, digits), format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
}

# Pre-compute formatted values used repeatedly in the text
price_eff      <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_level"))
price_pct      <- fmt_pct(get_mhs("price_effect_pct"))
avg_price_tr   <- fmt_d(get_mhs("avg_price_treated_pre"))
# Fixed-weight price index: basket definition, sample coverage, the
# composition decomposition, and the split by home size.
wt_single      <- formatC(get_mhs("base_wt_single"), format = "f", digits = 2)
wt_double      <- formatC(get_mhs("base_wt_double"), format = "f", digits = 2)
idx_base       <- fmt_d(get_mhs("idx_base_1993") / 1000)
avg_p_single   <- fmt_d(get_mhs("mean_price_single"))
avg_p_double   <- fmt_d(get_mhs("mean_price_double"))
price_ratio    <- formatC(get_mhs("price_ratio_double_single"),
                          format = "f", digits = 1)
n_index        <- format(as.integer(get_mhs("n_index")), big.mark = ",")
n_raw          <- format(as.integer(get_mhs("n_raw")), big.mark = ",")
n_dropped_mhs  <- as.integer(get_mhs("n_dropped_states"))
price_eff_raw     <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_raw_level"))
price_eff_raw_cmn <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_raw_cmn_level"))
price_eff_comp    <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_comp_level"))
share_dbl_eff  <- formatC(get_mhs("share_double_effect") * 100,
                          format = "f", digits = 2)
price_eff_single <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_single_level"))
price_eff_double <- fmt_d(get_mhs("price_effect_double_level"))
# Quantity side. Estimated on the same index sample as the price effects,
# so the two are read off one panel. Reported in log points: the static
# post-1994 coefficient, its standard error, and the implied 95% interval.
fmt_lp <- function(x, digits = 2) {
    paste0(if (x >= 0) "" else "-",
           formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = digits))
}
plc_eff    <- fmt_lp(get_mhs("placements_effect_static"))
plc_se     <- fmt_lp(get_mhs("placements_effect_static_se"))
plc_ci_lo  <- fmt_lp(get_mhs("placements_effect_static") -
                     1.96 * get_mhs("placements_effect_static_se"))
plc_ci_hi  <- fmt_lp(get_mhs("placements_effect_static") +
                     1.96 * get_mhs("placements_effect_static_se"))
n_plc      <- format(as.integer(get_mhs("n_placements")), big.mark = ",")
# Headline ATT: static post_mh coefficient (single precisely-estimated
# number), not the average of the event study's seven noisy period_constr
# x mh coefficients. The event study (bldg_dmg_evt_avg) is retained for
# describing pre-trends and the post-1994 ramp, not as the headline figure.
#
# The headline estimates are PROPORTIONAL (Poisson). Each coefficient is a log
# rate ratio on the conditional mean, so the percentage change is exp(b) - 1
# and NOT the coefficient itself; `pctc_fmt` below does that conversion and is
# used everywhere a percentage is quoted. Dollar figures come from
# `estimate-welfare.R`, which multiplies the ratio by an MH baseline mean --
# the pre-1994 mean for the private calculation and the post-1994 mean for the
# fiscal one, since the two have different counterfactuals.
pctc_fmt <- function(x, digits = 1) {
    paste0(if (x >= 0) "+" else "-",
           formatC(abs(100 * (exp(x) - 1)), format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
}
lp_fmt <- function(x, digits = 3) {
    paste0(if (x >= 0) "" else "-",
           formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = digits))
}
se_fmt <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
# Proportional effects, unsigned magnitude for prose that already says "lower".
bldg_dmg_pct   <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_static")) - 1)), 1)
cont_dmg_pct   <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_contents_damage_static")) - 1)), 1)
net_bldg_pct   <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_net_building_pmt_static")) - 1)), 1)
net_cont_pct   <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_net_contents_pmt_static")) - 1)), 1)
bldg_dmg_lp    <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_static"))
bldg_dmg_se    <- se_fmt(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_static_se"))
cont_dmg_lp    <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("pois_contents_damage_static"))
cont_dmg_se    <- se_fmt(get_nfip("pois_contents_damage_static_se"))
bldg_dmg_evt_avg <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_avg")) - 1)), 1)
# Dollar conversions, and the MH baseline means they are taken against.
bldg_dmg_eff   <- fmt_d(get_welf("delta_building"))
net_bldg_eff   <- fmt_d(get_welf("delta_building_pmt"))
net_cont_eff   <- fmt_d(get_welf("delta_contents_pmt"))
mh_pre_bldg    <- fmt_d(get_nfip("mh_pre_building_damage"))
mh_pre_cont    <- fmt_d(get_nfip("mh_pre_contents_damage"))
mh_post_nbldg  <- fmt_d(get_nfip("mh_post_net_building_pmt"))
mh_post_ncont  <- fmt_d(get_nfip("mh_post_net_contents_pmt"))
# The levels estimates the proportional ones replaced, for the appendix
# paragraph that reports how far the two scales diverge.
bldg_dmg_pct_unw <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_static_unw")) - 1)), 1)
cont_dmg_pct_unw <- fmt_pct(abs(100 * (exp(get_nfip("pois_contents_damage_static_unw")) - 1)), 1)
bldg_dmg_lvl   <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_static")))
bldg_dmg_lvl_se <- fmt_d(abs(get_nfip("building_damage_static_se")))
# County-specific housing-type effect. Staged but not yet quoted anywhere: the
# decision on whether this becomes a robustness column in the paper is open (see
# TODO.md Chunk O). The scalars are extracted here so that adding it is a text
# change rather than an estimation change.
bldg_ctymh_pct <- pctc_fmt(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_ctymh"))
bldg_ctymh_se  <- se_fmt(get_nfip("pois_building_damage_ctymh_se"))
cont_ctymh_pct <- pctc_fmt(get_nfip("pois_contents_damage_ctymh"))
cont_ctymh_se  <- se_fmt(get_nfip("pois_contents_damage_ctymh_se"))
nbldg_ctymh_pct <- pctc_fmt(get_nfip("pois_net_building_pmt_ctymh"))
nbldg_ctymh_se <- se_fmt(get_nfip("pois_net_building_pmt_ctymh_se"))
# Break-even for the omitted wind channel.
wind_be        <- fmt_d(get_welf("wind_breakeven_npv"))
wind_be_mult   <- formatC(get_welf("wind_breakeven_mult"), format = "f", digits = 1)
# Winsorization of the claim-level loss outcomes, for the table notes: the cap,

winsor_cap     <- fmt_d(get_nfip("winsor_cap"))
winsor_n_bldg  <- as.integer(get_nfip("winsor_n_building_damage"))
winsor_n_cont  <- as.integer(get_nfip("winsor_n_contents_damage"))

zero_pmt_bldg  <- fmt_pct(get_nfip("zero_share_net_building_pmt") * 100, 0)

claim_rate_fmt <- fmt_pct(get_welf("claim_rate_pooled_pre") * 100, 1)
ann_benefit    <- fmt_d(get_welf("annual_benefit"))
npv_baseline   <- fmt_d(get_welf("npv_3pct_20yr"))
bcr_pct        <- fmt_pct(get_welf("bcr_3pct_20yr") * 100)
# Raw-LaTeX-escaped copy: the `\begin{abstract}` block below is a raw LaTeX

# An unescaped "%" there starts a LaTeX comment and truncates the rest of

bcr_pct_tex    <- sub("%", "\\\\%", bcr_pct)

n_mh_claims    <- format(as.integer(get_ss("total_claims_mh")), big.mark = ",")

# Take-up per housing-unit stock (Chunk E; third margin added in Chunk I;
# moved to Poisson counts with an exposure offset in Chunk N).
#
# All three take-up coefficients are now LOG RATE RATIOS -- proportional

# 1,000 homes that the earlier ratio regressions produced. The scalar names
# carry a `_ppml` marker for exactly that reason, so a coefficient cannot be
# quoted on the wrong scale by reusing an old name. Percent conversions use
# exp(b) - 1 rather than treating the coefficient as a percentage, since
# several of these are large enough for the difference to show.
signed_fmt <- function(x, digits = 1) {
    paste0(if (x >= 0) "+" else "-",
           formatC(abs(round(x, digits)), format = "f", digits = digits))
}
lp_fmt  <- function(x, digits = 3) signed_fmt(x, digits)
se_fmt  <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pctc_fmt <- function(x, digits = 1) {
    paste0(if (x >= 0) "+" else "-",
           formatC(abs(100 * (exp(x) - 1)), format = "f", digits = digits), "%")
}
# Column (1), take-up: the static contrast, its state- and county-clustered

tk_stc      <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("takeup_ppml_static"))

cr_ci_lo    <- pctc_fmt(get_nfip("claim_rate_ppml_static") -

cr_ci_hi    <- pctc_fmt(get_nfip("claim_rate_ppml_static") +

# Pre-1994 MH levels of the three margins, quoted so the log coefficients

ppl_home_base  <- formatC(get_nfip("policies_per_1k_homes_yr_base_mh"),

clmrate_base   <- formatC(get_nfip("claim_rate_base_mh") * 1000,

lvl_fmt <- function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
ppl_mh_pre   <- lvl_fmt(get_nfip("policies_per_1k_homes_yr_mh_pre"))
ppl_mh_post  <- lvl_fmt(get_nfip("policies_per_1k_homes_yr_mh_post"))

tk_nogeo     <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("takeup_ppml_static_nogeo"))

tk_mand_contrib <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("takeup_mand_share_pre_mh") *

# Flat-denominator perturbation (Chunk N): the same specification with the

tk_flat_stc     <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("takeup_ppml_static_flat"))

ch_flat_stc     <- lp_fmt(get_nfip("claims_home_ppml_static_flat"))

# Specification diagnostics for the levels-vs-counts paragraph. The level

lvl_fmt2      <- function(x) signed_fmt(x, 2)
tk_lvl_stc    <- lvl_fmt2(get_nfip("takeup_lvl_static"))

wd_n_bins        <- as.integer(get_nfip("water_depth_n_bins"))

wd_one_bin       <- fmt_pct(get_nfip("water_depth_single_bin_share") * 100, 1)
```

\begin{abstract}
Does mandated climate adaptation pay for itself? I study the 1994 HUD wind standard reform, which required structural upgrades to manufactured homes in hurricane-prone areas. Using claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP), I compare flood damage to manufactured and site-built homes of different construction vintages exposed to floods in the same county and over the same period. Manufactured homes built after 1994 experience `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage per claim relative to site-built homes of the same vintage, which is `r bldg_dmg_eff` against the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean. On the cost side, the reform raised manufactured home prices by `r price_eff` in treated states. A back-of-envelope calculation suggests the insured flood channel alone recovers roughly `r bcr_pct_tex` of the upfront cost; the total return---including wind damage, uninsured losses, and reduced risk---is likely higher, but this paper does not measure those channels. For the 22 million Americans living in manufactured homes, many of whom are low-income and lack disaster insurance, the HUD standard functions as built-in catastrophe insurance: it reduces risk automatically, without requiring annual premium payments, claims filing, or compliance with eligibility rules that many manufactured homeowners cannot meet.
\end{abstract}

# Introduction

The U.S. experienced over 100 billion-dollar climate disasters over the five years before 2026, incurring damages of over \$600 billion dollars.[^billion-dollar] These costs are projected to grow substantially as climate change intensifies extreme weather events. Building codes and other forms of mandated adaptation investment are a potential policy tool for reducing disaster losses and risk, but the returns to these investments are not well understood, and they may have indirect effects on household's exposure to climate risk by interacting with insurance markets. This paper provides new evidence on the costs and benefits of mandated adaptation in the context of manufactured housing (MH), a sector that is both highly vulnerable to climate risk and largely -- though not entirely -- uninsured.[^mh]

[^billion-dollar]: Climate Central. "U.S. Billion-Dollar Weather and Climate Disasters." ClimateCentral.Org, 2026. \href{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}{https://www.climatecentral.org/climate-services/billion-dollar-disasters/summary-stats}.

[^mh]: "Manufactured homes" are the preferred industry term and refer specifically to mobile homes that satisfy the 1976 HUD Code. As the vast majority of mobile homes produced since 1976 satisfy the code, I use the terms "manufactured" and "mobile" interchangeably.

Government mandates for costly adaptation may be justified if private take-up is hindered by frictions. For instance, households may misperceive climate risk [@bakkensen_going_2022; @gallagher_learning_2014]. They may fail to internalize benefits to their neighbors [@baylis_mandated_2021]. They may enjoy limited upside from adaptation if mitigation behaviors are not reflected in insurance premiums [@wagner_adaptation_2022]. Finally, they may rely on public insurance programs and disaster relief instead [@deryugina_fiscal_2017; @baylis_moral_2019].

I estimate both the direct cost of compliance, in the form of additional construction costs; and the direct benefits, in reduced flood damage. My results indicate that benefits from the single channel of flood damage reduction do not outweigh the considerable cost of the reform. However, it is possible that accounting for other benefits, such as the insurance value and non-flooding damages, would yield a positive private benefit-cost ratio.

On the cost side, I use the Census Bureau's Manufactured Housing Survey to estimate a difference-in-differences comparing manufactured home prices in states with HUD wind zones II and III (treated) to zone I states (control), before and after 1994. Prices in treated states rose by `r price_eff`, an increase of roughly `r price_pct` on an average of `r avg_price_tr` in treated states. There is no detectable effect on placements, though point estimates are imprecise. A price increase without an accompanying decline in quantity is consistent with a world where households value the HUD-mandated improvements roughly at cost.

On the benefit side, I use flood insurance claim and policy data from the National Flood Insurance Program (NFIP) to estimate the effect of the HUD standard on flood damage. My identification strategy exploits two sources of variation: MH versus site-built housing, and post-1994 versus pre-1994 construction vintage. County by flood-loss-period fixed effects ensure comparisons are made only between homes exposed to the same floods in the same location. This is a double-difference in vintage and housing type: the site-built comparison group absorbs secular changes in construction quality and storm severity, isolating the manufactured-home-specific break at 1994.

Post-1994 manufactured homes experience `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage per claim relative to pre-1994 manufactured homes, compared to the same vintage difference for site-built homes. The estimates are proportional rather than absolute, for reasons set out in Section \ref{results}: manufactured and site-built homes differ in value by a factor of roughly two and a half, and a specification in dollars is not identified in its own units when the effect it estimates is a percentage. Against a pre-1994 manufactured-home mean of `r mh_pre_bldg` per claim, the proportional estimate is `r bldg_dmg_eff`. The event study shows the effect emerging at 1994 and growing with later construction cohorts, consistent with delays between the manufacture and installation of MH, though the pre-1994 coefficients wander enough that the break is less sharp than the static estimate alone suggests. Contents damage falls by `r cont_dmg_pct` and contents payments by `r net_cont_pct`. At the same time, MH policies for post-1994 vintages are more likely to be located in Special Flood Hazard Areas, and carry higher replacement costs and building coverage, all of which would tend to increase expected NFIP payments. These compositional shifts run against the estimated damage reductions rather than producing them.

Combining costs and benefits at the unit level yields a back-of-envelope private cost-benefit calculation for the purchaser of a post-1994 manufactured home. Among insured MH in the NFIP data, the pre-1994 annual claim rate is roughly `r claim_rate_fmt`. Applied to per-claim reductions of `r delta_bldg` in building damages and `r delta_cont` in contents damages, this implies an expected annual damage reduction of `r ann_benefit`, or `r npv_baseline` discounting at 3% over a 20-year MH lifespan. Expected savings from reduced flood damage alone are roughly `r bcr_pct` of the `r cost_fmt` price increase. This is a statement about which channel is measured, not a verdict on the standard: the regulation is a wind standard, and the flood channel estimated here is the one the data can identify. Closing the gap would require the wind channel to deliver `r wind_be` in present value, or `r wind_be_mult` times the measured flood benefit---a threshold this paper states but does not test.

At the aggregate level, the reform generates meaningful fiscal spillovers. The point estimates imply reductions of `r net_bldg_pct` in net building payments and `r net_cont_pct` in net contents payments per MH claim, or `r net_bldg_eff` and `r net_cont_eff` against the observed post-1994 manufactured-home means of `r mh_post_nbldg` and `r mh_post_ncont`. Applied to the `r n_post_claims` claims on MH built between 1994 and 1999 observed in the NFIP sample, this yields roughly `r nfip_sav_m` in direct NFIP payment savings---a conservative figure that conditions on filing a claim and does not scale to the full stock of post-reform MH.[^fiscal-nfip] Spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster relief---most notably FEMA Individual Assistance, SBA disaster loans, and state emergency grants---are likely substantially larger. <!--\textcolor{red}{[PLACEHOLDER: estimate of \emph{ex post} disaster relief spillover to be added.]}-->

[^fiscal-nfip]: The `r n_post_claims` claims for MH built 1994-1999 are observed over loss years 1994-2023. This calculation assumes no change in claim frequency or policy take-up and applies the main-specification payment reductions to the observed claim count.

This paper contributes to several literatures. First, it provides direct evidence on the returns to building code regulation for disaster resilience. @simmons_economic_2018 and @dehring_coastal_2013 study whether building code reforms in Florida for site-built homes improved resilience to hurricanes and find conflicting results. For manufactured housing, my results support a body of descriptive work examining the 1994 HUD code reform [@simmons_manufactured_2008; @kevin_r_grosskopf_manufactured_2005].

Methodologically, @baylis_mandated_2021 implement a similar study of wildfire building codes in California and find large benefits to mandatory adaptation, with fiscal spillovers and insurance value potentially justifying tighter building codes even in areas with moderate wildfire risk. This paper improves on their empirical strategy by exploiting the fact that manufactured homes are regulated federally, allowing me to disentangle building code reforms from general vintage effects. Specifically, I compare site-built and manufactured homes in the same area, exposed to the same floods, and built in the same year. My design builds on the set of methodologies used in the economics literature to study building codes, which generally rely on across-vintage or across-location comparisons [@jacobsen_are_2013; @levinson_how_2016]. My approach can be applied to any context where different housing types are subject to different regulatory bodies.

I also contribute to a rich literature evaluating the fiscal position of the National Flood Insurance Program and the broader fiscal consequences of natural disasters. My results suggest that HUD code reforms had moderate fiscal spillovers on the NFIP through reduced payouts on post-1994 MH claims, and likely larger spillovers on \emph{ex post} disaster relief programs that serve the largely uninsured MH population [@solomon_optimal_2026].

The scope of this paper is limited to only one channel of benefits -- flood damage reduction -- and does not attempt to estimate other benefits (e.g., wind damage reduction, spillovers to adjacent homes, reduced displacement, fiscal spillovers to \emph{ex post} disaster assistance). I leave the estimation of these channels to future work.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section \ref{institutional-background} describes the institutional background and the 1994 HUD Code reform. Section \ref{data} describes the data. Section \ref{empirical-strategy} presents the empirical strategy. Section \ref{results} reports the results, and Section \ref{conclusion} concludes.

# Institutional Background

## Manufactured Housing and the HUD Code

Approximately 6% of the housing stock are manufactured homes. This share is substantially higher in rural areas and in the Southeast, where the share of MH can exceed 15%.[^mh-stats] These homes are disproportionately occupied by low-income households, and they are disproportionately exposed to natural disaster risk. In 1992, Hurricane Andrew destroyed 97% of manufactured homes in its path in Dade County, Florida, compared to 11% of site-built homes.[^florida-case]

[^florida-case]: *Florida Manufactured Housing Ass'n v. Cisneros*, 53 F.3d 1565 (11th Cir. 1995).

[^mh-stats]: Manufactured-Housing Consumer Finance in the U.S. Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, 2014. https://www.consumerfinance.gov/data-research/research-reports/manufactured-housing-consumer-finance-in-the-u-s/. Manufactured homes are built in a factory and transported to a site, as distinct from site-built (stick-built) homes constructed on location.

The vulnerability of manufactured homes to extreme weather prompted a major regulatory response. In 1994, HUD revised the Manufactured Home Construction and Safety Standards---the federal building code governing all manufactured housing---to impose wind resistance requirements. The reform created a three-zone wind classification system and required structural upgrades for homes sited in high-wind zones, including stronger anchoring and strapping, upgraded sheathing and fastening schedules, and wind-pressure requirements for components and cladding. Unlike local building codes for site-built homes, the HUD Code is a federal minimum standard that preempts state and local regulation.

The preemption of local codes is a distinctive feature of the manufactured housing market. Site-built homes are subject to state and local building codes, which vary substantially across jurisdictions and are enforced through local permitting and inspection processes. Manufactured homes, by contrast, must meet a single federal standard. This institutional feature is central to the identification strategy: the 1994 reform was implemented through the federal HUD Code for manufactured homes, with wind-resistance requirements varying by HUD wind zone, while site-built homes remained governed by state and local codes. The reform was national in administration but not uniform in intensity---the binding upgrades applied to units sited in zones II and III---and the cost design in Section \ref{empirical-strategy} exploits exactly that differential exposure.

## NFIP and Flood Insurance for Manufactured Homes

The National Flood Insurance Program provides federally backed flood insurance to property owners in participating communities. Flood insurance is mandatory for properties with federally backed mortgages in FEMA-designated Special Flood Hazard Areas (SFHAs). The requirement turns on the lending channel and the covered security property rather than on the label attached to the financing. Manufactured homes are frequently financed with chattel loans (personal property loans secured by the home but not the land), many of which fall outside the federally regulated or federally connected lending that triggers mandatory purchase. Reduced exposure to the mandate is one reason NFIP take-up among manufactured homeowners is substantially lower than among site-built homeowners in comparable flood zones.

The NFIP data used in this paper record claims and policy information at the individual level. This allows direct comparison of flood damage outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes conditional on holding NFIP coverage. The selection into flood insurance coverage is a potential concern that I address through composition checks on the insured population in Section \ref{selection-and-composition}.

# Data

## Manufactured Housing Prices and Shipments

I estimate the price and quantity effects using a state-by-year panel from the Census Bureau's Manufactured Housing Survey (MHS), which reports average sales prices and placement counts by state. I focus on the period immediately around the HUD code change, 1988 - 2000. The treatment group consists of states containing HUD wind zones II or III; the control group is zone I states (see Figure \ref{map:treated-states}).

Manufactured homes are placed in two sizes. A single-section home arrives as one transportable unit; a multi-section home arrives as two or more units that are joined on site. Multi-section homes are larger and more expensive: over the sample period the average real sales price is `r avg_p_single` for a single-section home and `r avg_p_double` for a multi-section home, a ratio of `r price_ratio` to one. The survey reports an average sales price for each size separately and an average across all homes placed. The all-homes average is the placement-weighted mixture of the two size-specific averages, so it rises both when prices rise and when placements shift toward multi-section homes. The multi-section share differs across states and changes over the sample period, so the all-homes average conflates price changes with changes in the size mix, and a shift in the mix would enter a difference-in-differences estimate as a price effect.

I therefore construct a fixed-weight price index. Let $p^{S}_{st}$ and $p^{D}_{st}$ denote the average real sales price of single-section and multi-section homes in state $s$ and year $t$. The index is

\begin{equation}
P_{st} = \omega^{S} p^{S}_{st} + \omega^{D} p^{D}_{st},
\label{eq:price-index}
\end{equation}

where $\omega^{S}$ and $\omega^{D}$ are the shares of single- and multi-section homes among all homes placed nationally between 1988 and 1993, the six years preceding the reform. These weights are `r wt_single` and `r wt_double`, and they are held fixed across all states and all years. The index is therefore the cost of a fixed basket of homes: it changes only when the price of a size changes, and by construction no variation in the size mix, either across states or over time, can enter it. I report the index normalized so that its national 1993 value equals 100. The normalization divides the index by the single constant `r idx_base`, so the normalized and dollar-denominated versions of the index give the same estimates in different units.

Constructing the index requires both size-specific averages. The survey suppresses these for states with few placements, so the index is defined for `r n_index` of the `r n_raw` state-years in which the all-homes average is published. The excluded state-years are small states, predominantly in the control group. The quantity analysis uses these same state-years, even though placement counts are published more widely, so that the price and quantity effects are estimated on one sample and can be read together. All specifications are weighted by the state's average number of shipments between 1988 and 1993; `r n_dropped_mhs` states with no recorded shipments over that period are dropped from the sample.

## Flood Damage and Insurance Coverage

I use two datasets from FEMA on individual flood insurance claims and policy records. Claims data record the date of loss, construction year, building and contents damage amounts, NFIP payments, property characteristics, and the census tract. Policy data record coverage amounts, premium, property characteristics, and flood zone designation. Both datasets include a field identifying manufactured homes.

### Final Sample

I restrict the sample to homes with construction years between 1984 and 1999 and loss dates from 1994 onward. I further restrict both the claims and policy data to detached single-family residential properties, using the occupancy classification recorded in each dataset; this excludes multi-unit residential buildings and non-residential structures from the site-built comparison group, and non-residential manufactured homes from the manufactured-home group, using the same classification on both sides. Because claims for manufactured homes are relatively rare, I bin both the construction year and loss year in two and five year periods, respectively, to improve power. The construction-year window is chosen so that the two-year construction bins are anchored on 1992--1993 as the last pre-reform bin and every bin contains two full construction years. The window also matches the range over which the housing-stock denominator of Section \ref{appendix-take-up} is defined.

For the policy analysis, I construct a balanced panel at the census tract $\times$ calendar-period $\times$ housing-type $\times$ construction-period level, which I aggregate to the county level for estimation. Policy records begin in 2009, so the policy panel spans the three five-year calendar periods 2009--2013, 2014--2018, and 2019--2023; claims are assigned to the same calendar periods, so a single period index serves both. Each cell reports the number of policy-years observed during the period along with the policy-weighted average of their characteristics. A policy-year is one policy term, assigned to the calendar year containing the midpoint of its coverage period; a home insured continuously for all five years of a period therefore contributes five policy-years to that cell. The panel is balanced over housing type and construction period within tract-periods that have positive policy exposure, so cells with zero claims but at least one policy-year are retained and contribute a zero to the claim rate. Cells with zero policy-years have no defined claim rate or average policy characteristics; they are dropped from every cell-level regression in this paper, including those of Section \ref{appendix-take-up}, whose outcomes are counts of policy-years and claims per unit of exposure and so require positive exposure.

The policy-composition results of Section \ref{selection-and-composition} use a separate extract of the same underlying policy data, at the level of the individual policy term rather than aggregated to the tract-period cell, restricted to the same construction-vintage window, calendar periods, and single-family residential occupancy classification described above.

All nominal values are deflated to constant (2000) dollars using the CPI-U. I restrict both samples to the continental US. Table \ref{tab:sumstats-nfip} reports summary statistics for the NFIP data by construction vintage and housing type. Manufactured homes generally experience lower building and contents damage than site-built homes, with correspondingly lower coverage amounts. I observe `r n_mh_claims` claims for manufactured homes in the sample, or roughly `r mh_claim_pct`% of all claims, substantially lower than the share of manufactured homes in the overall housing stock \citep{genz_why_2001}.

# Empirical Strategy

## Cost Estimation

I estimate the effect of the 1994 HUD standard on manufactured home prices using a two-way fixed effects event study:

\begin{equation}
P_{st} = \alpha_s + \gamma_t + \sum_{k \neq 1993} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\text{year} = k] \times \text{Treated}_s) + \varepsilon_{st}
\label{eq:event-study-cost}
\end{equation}

where $P_{st}$ is the fixed-weight price index of Equation \eqref{eq:price-index} for state $s$ in year $t$, $\alpha_s$ and $\gamma_t$ are state and year fixed effects, and $\text{Treated}_s$ indicates states containing wind zones II or III. The 1993 interaction is omitted: with state fixed effects the full set of treated-by-year interactions is collinear with the time-invariant treated indicator. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore trace out the price difference between treated and control states relative to 1993. All MHS specifications, including this one, are weighted by the state's average number of shipments between 1988 and 1993. Standard errors are clustered by state.

## Benefit Estimation: Event Study

The primary benefit-side specification is an event study that imposes no functional form on the vintage profile:

\begin{equation}
Y_{it} = \alpha_{c(i),t} + \delta_m + \lambda_{\nu_i} + \sum_{k \neq 1992} \beta_k (\mathbf{1}[\nu_i = k] \times \text{MH}_i) + \varepsilon_{it}
\label{eq:event-study-benefit}
\end{equation}

where $Y_{it}$ is the outcome for claim $i$ (e.g., building damage), $\alpha_{c(i),t}$ is a county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect absorbing location-specific storm severity, $\delta_m$ is a manufactured housing indicator absorbing time-invariant differences between housing types, $\text{MH}_i$ is an indicator for manufactured homes, and $\nu_i$ is the construction vintage bin of home $i$. The term $\lambda_{\nu_i}$ is a full set of construction-vintage fixed effects common to both housing types, so that the interactions are identified off deviations from the common vintage profile rather than off the level of that profile. The coefficients $\beta_k$ therefore capture the manufactured-home-specific vintage profile relative to the omitted 1992--1993 reference bin. Post-1994 coefficients are reduced-form cohort effects of exposure to the reform: because construction vintage is a proxy for actual regulatory exposure, the earliest post-reform bins are potentially attenuated by production-installation lags and incomplete compliance.

Identification relies on a parallel trends assumption in the vintage profile of outcomes between manufactured and site-built homes in the absence of the HUD code reform. In other words, homes built at different times may experience different levels of flood damage due to changes in construction quality, storm severity, or intra-county location, but these vintage effects should be the same for manufactured and site-built homes. I support this assumption by showing flat pre-trends in the event study specification across a broad range of claim-level and cell-level outcomes.

I expect the cohort effects to grow with later construction cohorts as compliance rates increase. Because of lags between production and installation, some units with post-1994 installation dates may have been manufactured before the regulation went into effect in July of 1994.

The cell-level specifications replace the county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect in Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit} with a county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effect, since the cell panel is aggregated to five-year periods; regressions are weighted by the number of policies in the cell. The policy panel is described in Section \ref{data}.

# Results {#results}

## Cost Side: Manufactured Home Prices

Figure \ref{fig:es-price} presents the event study for the fixed-weight manufactured home price index. Prior to 1994, treated and control states follow parallel trends: the pre-treatment coefficients are small, precisely estimated, and statistically indistinguishable from zero. The index diverges after 1993 and separates fully from 1995 onward, with treated states experiencing an average post-1994 increase of `r price_eff`. The effect is economically large, corresponding to an `r price_pct` increase on a pre-reform index level of `r avg_price_tr` in treated states.

The 1994 coefficient is small relative to those that follow, and the separation appears from 1995. This is what the timing of the reform implies: the standard took effect in July 1994, so only part of that year's placements were subject to it, and lags between production and installation push further compliance into 1995. The persistence of the premium through 2000 shows that the price gap was not a one-year implementation spike; its source---higher marginal production costs, fixed redesign costs amortized over many units, quality upgrading, or demand-side valuation of the improved construction---is not pinned down by the price path alone.

Because the outcome holds the size mix fixed, this estimate cannot reflect a shift in the composition of placements toward more expensive multi-section homes. Two comparisons show how much that restriction matters. First, holding the sample fixed, the all-homes average sales price yields `r price_eff_raw_cmn` against the index's `r price_eff`; valuing each state-year's actual size mix at fixed national prices, so that the mix shift is the only source of variation, yields `r price_eff_comp`, and the treated-control difference in the multi-section share after 1994 is `r share_dbl_eff` percentage points. The size mix therefore accounts for almost none of the price effect. Second, estimated on every state-year for which it is published rather than only those where the index is defined, the all-homes average yields `r price_eff_raw`. The gap between that figure and the index estimate is driven by the small states that drop out when both size-specific prices are required, not by composition.

I also find that price effects are larger for multi-section units (`r price_eff_double`) than for single-section units (`r price_eff_single`), suggesting that part of the compliance cost varies with the size of the unit rather than being a fixed charge per home (Table \ref{tab:mhs-section-type}).

Figure \ref{fig:es-placements} shows the corresponding event study for log placements, estimated on the same state-years as the price index so that the price and quantity effects describe one panel rather than two. Collapsing the post-period to a single coefficient gives `r plc_eff` log points (SE `r plc_se`), a 95% interval of `r plc_ci_lo` to `r plc_ci_hi`. The point estimate is positive and statistically indistinguishable from zero, so the data do not show a decline in the quantity of manufactured homes shipped to treated states. The interval is wide enough to contain declines of roughly `r fmt_lp(abs(get_mhs("placements_effect_static") - 1.96 * get_mhs("placements_effect_static_se")))` log points as well as increases, so a modest decline cannot be ruled out. The estimates are consistent with relatively inelastic demand, or with an outward demand shift from the improved construction offsetting the higher price.

## Benefit Side: Flood Damage

### Post 1994 MH experience lower flood damages

Figure \ref{fig:es-building-damage} presents the event study for building damage per claim. Every coefficient is a proportional change in expected damage, for reasons given below. The pre-1994 coefficients are small and change sign across bins, without a trend toward the reform. Beginning with the 1994 construction cohort, manufactured homes experience lower building damage relative to site-built homes, averaging `r bldg_dmg_evt_avg` across the three post-reform bins and growing slightly with later cohorts as compliance ramps up. The pre-1994 coefficients are not all negligible relative to the post-1994 ones, so the profile establishes that the effect appears at 1994 rather than that nothing whatever moves before it.

Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static} collapses this vintage profile to a single pre/post-1994 comparison: manufactured homes built after 1994 experience `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage per claim than site-built homes of the same vintage (coefficient `r bldg_dmg_lp`, standard error `r bldg_dmg_se`). Applied to the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean of `r mh_pre_bldg` per claim, this is a reduction of `r bldg_dmg_eff`. I report the static estimate as the headline number, since it is a single precisely-estimated average treatment effect rather than an average of seven individually-noisy event-study coefficients; the event study itself remains the vehicle for showing the vintage profile.

Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes} presents supplementary outcomes on insurance payments and damage to the building's contents. Contents damage declines by `r cont_dmg_pct` (coefficient `r cont_dmg_lp`, standard error `r cont_dmg_se`), contents payments by `r net_cont_pct`, and net building payments by `r net_bldg_pct`, consistent with improved structural integrity. Because the four outcomes are proportional changes in quantities with different means, the ordering among them in percentage terms is not the ordering in dollars: net building payments fall by a smaller percentage than building damage but from a large base, while net contents payments fall by the largest percentage from the smallest base. Policy limits and deductibles break the link between a loss and the amount the program pays, which is why the payment columns and the damage columns need not agree.

### Why the estimates are proportional

All four claim-level outcomes are estimated as proportional changes rather than as dollar differences. This is not a presentational choice, and an earlier version of this paper made the opposite one, so the reason is worth stating.

The vintage effect these outcomes share is proportional, not additive. Manufactured and site-built homes differ in replacement cost by a factor of roughly two and a half. Any common force that changes damage by a percentage---a construction-cost trend, a change in what floods do to a house of a given quality---therefore changes it by different dollar amounts for the two housing types. A specification in dollars asks a single housing-type fixed effect to absorb a gap that is proportional, which it cannot do, and the treatment coefficient absorbs the residual. The size of the problem is not hypothetical. On simulated claims built with a treatment effect of exactly zero, but with the proportional housing-type gap and vintage gradient these data display, the dollar specification returns a large and statistically significant negative coefficient while the Poisson specification returns zero. The two specifications also disagree on the real data by about the margin that exercise predicts: the dollar estimate for building damage is `r bldg_dmg_lvl` (SE `r bldg_dmg_lvl_se`), while the proportional estimate applied to the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean is `r bldg_dmg_eff`. The gap between those two figures is the misspecification, not a finding.

Among proportional specifications I use Poisson regression rather than a regression on logged damage. Three properties matter. Poisson admits zeros natively, which the payment outcomes require: `r zero_pmt_bldg` of claims record a zero net building payment and `r zero_pmt_cont` a zero net contents payment, so a log specification would drop them and would estimate the damage and payment columns on different samples. It requires no retransformation, so the estimate can be stated without an assumption about the shape of the loss distribution. Most importantly for what follows, Poisson models the conditional mean directly, so the exponentiated coefficient is a ratio of expected dollar losses. Multiplying an observed mean by it therefore recovers a dollar figure, which is what the cost-benefit calculation of Section \ref{cost-benefit} needs and what a regression on logged damage would not supply---there the exponentiated coefficient is a ratio of geometric means, and converting it into a change in the mean requires exactly the distributional assumption the levels specification was originally chosen to avoid.

The claim-level loss and payment fields are otherwise well behaved, unlike the assessed-value and replacement-cost fields discussed in Section \ref{selection-and-composition}. Net payments are bounded by the program's statutory coverage limits.

The two damage fields are not bounded and contain a small number of records far outside any plausible single-family loss, so all four outcomes are winsorized at `r winsor_cap`. The cap binds for `r winsor_n_bldg` building-damage records and `r winsor_n_cont` contents-damage records out of more than two hundred thousand, for no payment records, and for no manufactured home. It moves the proportional building-damage coefficient from `r bldg_dmg_pct_unw` to `r bldg_dmg_pct`, and the contents-damage coefficient from `r cont_dmg_pct_unw` to `r cont_dmg_pct`. Neither movement changes any conclusion. Poisson weights an observation by its fitted mean rather than by its squared deviation, so a handful of extreme records moves it less than it moves a regression in dollars. The cap is retained because the affected records are not plausible losses, not because the estimates depend on it.

## Selection and Composition {#selection-and-composition}

A concern with the vintage-based design is that post-1994 manufactured home policyholders may differ systematically from pre-1994 policyholders, and that these compositional differences rather than construction quality drive the damage results. Table \ref{tab:composition} reports event studies for five policy characteristics, estimated on individual policy terms rather than on the cell-level panel used elsewhere in this section, restricted like the claims and policy samples throughout to single-family residential properties, and using the same vintage bins and reference bin (1992--1993) as the damage event studies.

All five outcomes are estimated by Poisson pseudo-maximum-likelihood (PPML), for the reasons given in Section \ref{results} for the claim-level damage and payment outcomes: the vintage effect a common force exerts on these outcomes is proportional rather than additive, and PPML models the conditional mean directly, so every coefficient in the table is a log rate ratio on the same scale regardless of the outcome's own units. This choice matters most for replacement cost. Recorded replacement cost is not bounded: its standard deviation across policy terms is more than ten times its mean, and its maximum exceeds one billion dollars for a single-family home. A specification in dollar levels lets those records dominate the fit, explaining almost none of the variance and producing an unstable vintage profile; an earlier version of this table instead logged the outcome, which fits better but drops every policy term with a zero recorded replacement cost. PPML weights an observation by its fitted mean rather than by its squared deviation, so the extreme records no longer dominate, and the outcome enters as a level like the other four. The `r repl_zero_pct` of policy terms recording an exact replacement cost of zero are still dropped, since a zero replacement cost on an insured single-family home is a recording convention rather than a measurement, independent of which estimator reads the column. Coverage amounts are additionally bounded above by the program's statutory limits, so their dispersion is modest. The two location and design indicators (elevated building, Special Flood Hazard Area) enter as 0/1 rather than rescaled to percentage points, since under PPML a constant rescaling of the outcome is absorbed by the fixed effects and leaves the estimated coefficients unchanged; the percentage-point rescaling used in an earlier, OLS-based version of this table only made those coefficients comparable in magnitude to the dollar columns, which PPML's common log-point scale already does.

Contents coverage enters unconditionally, with policies carrying no contents coverage recorded as zero. An earlier version of this table separated the probability of carrying any contents coverage from the amount carried conditional on carrying some. Both margins are individually indistinguishable from zero after 1994, so the single unconditional column reports the same finding, and it avoids conditioning on a variable that itself varies across vintages.

Two patterns appear. The first concerns the pre-1994 vintages, and here the profile is a set of isolated departures rather than a single trend shared across outcomes. Building coverage is significantly lower for manufactured homes than for site-built homes of the same vintage in the earliest pre-1994 bin (1984--1985) and statistically indistinguishable from zero in the three bins that follow it. Contents coverage moves in the opposite direction and at the opposite end of the pre-1994 window: it is statistically indistinguishable from zero in the three earliest pre-1994 bins and significantly higher only in the bin immediately preceding the reference period (1990--1991). Replacement cost shows no pre-1994 gap that clears conventional significance at any bin. The elevated-building share is likewise flat throughout the pre-1994 period. The outcome moving in a different direction from all of these is location: the share of manufactured home policies in a Special Flood Hazard Area is significantly lower than site-built in two of the four pre-1994 bins (1986--1987 and 1990--1991), with a third (1988--1989) significant only at the 10% level, and it does not shrink toward zero approaching the reference bin. The persistence of the Special Flood Hazard Area gap across most of the pre-1994 period means the parallel-vintage-trends assumption is less well supported for that outcome than for the damage outcomes, where the pre-1994 coefficients are flat and near zero; the other composition outcomes, whose pre-1994 departures are each confined to a single bin, do not raise the same concern.

The second pattern concerns the post-1994 vintages, which are the ones that bear on the damage estimates. Three outcomes move in a direction that would raise, not lower, expected flood damage for post-1994 manufactured homes: building coverage is significantly higher in all three post-1994 bins and rises across them, replacement cost is significantly higher in the first two post-1994 bins and marginally significant (10% level) in the third, declining across the three rather than remaining stable, and the share of policies in a Special Flood Hazard Area is significantly higher in all three and rises monotonically across them. Contents coverage shows no significant post-1994 shift. The elevated-building share is statistically indistinguishable from zero in the first two post-1994 bins and only marginally significant (10% level) in the last.

These post-1994 shifts work against the main result. Higher building coverage and higher replacement cost mechanically raise the payment a given flood can generate, and concentration in Special Flood Hazard Areas raises flood exposure itself; all three would tend to increase measured damage for post-1994 manufactured homes, not lower it. The elevated-building share is the one shift that works in the direction of the main result, and, as before, it moves only for the latest construction vintage in the sample, where it is significant only at the 10% level. Its timing matters: because the increase appears well after 1994, elevation cannot account for the damage reductions estimated in the 1994 and 1996 bins, and it can bear on the interpretation only of the last cohort, and only weakly at that. For that cohort elevation is plausibly part of the treatment channel---the HUD Code encouraged improved siting and installation practices---rather than a confound.

I therefore read the post-1994 composition of insured manufactured homes as shifting toward higher, not lower, expected flood damage, and read the damage estimates as understating the effect of construction quality by whatever amount that shift contributes. This reading now rests on three outcomes moving together in the same direction rather than one, and I still do not treat it as a quantitative bound.

A further channel is the size of the insured pool rather than its observed characteristics. If a larger share of post-1994 manufactured homes carries an NFIP policy, the post-1994 insured pool is a less selected share of the underlying stock, and the damage estimates compare pools selected to different degrees. Section \ref{appendix-take-up} estimates the size of that shift and cannot reject zero: the fraction of manufactured homes holding a policy changes by `r tk_stc_pct` after 1994 relative to site-built homes of the same vintage, with a 95\% interval running from `r tk_ci_lo` to `r tk_ci_hi`. That interval is wide enough to admit a shift in either direction, and the sign of the resulting bias would in any case depend on how the homes drawn into coverage compare with those already insured, which these data do not identify. Unlike the coverage and location shifts above, this channel is unsigned, and I note it as a limitation rather than as a bound.

A separate concern operates through flood severity itself rather than through policy characteristics: if post-1994 manufactured homes are flooded to different depths than pre-1994 manufactured homes or than site-built homes of the same vintage, the damage reduction could reflect differential exposure rather than construction quality. Section \ref{appendix-water-depth} adds water depth at the time of loss as a control, and reports both the resulting estimate and how it varies with housing type. The result is close to the baseline and does not depend on flood severity in a way that would account for the main finding.

The main building damage results rely on county $\times$ loss-period fixed effects to absorb location-specific variation in storm severity. A concern is that within-county variation in flood exposure---for instance, proximity to a floodplain or drainage infrastructure---could differ systematically across construction vintages and housing types. I address this by re-estimating the primary building damage specification with census tract $\times$ loss-period fixed effects, which absorb finer-grained geographic heterogeneity.

# Discussion

## Cost-Benefit

The cost and benefit estimates can be combined in a back-of-envelope calculation. The per-unit compliance cost is approximately `r cost_fmt`, paid once at purchase.

The benefit estimates are proportional, so converting them into dollars requires a baseline to apply them to, and the choice of baseline follows from the counterfactual each calculation poses. This section asks what a buyer of a post-1994 home saves relative to an otherwise identical pre-1994 home, and it applies the pre-1994 claim rate as the counterfactual hazard; the damage figure must therefore be the pre-1994 manufactured-home mean. That is `r mh_pre_bldg` per claim for building damage and `r mh_pre_cont` for contents. Applying the estimated reductions of `r bldg_dmg_pct` and `r cont_dmg_pct` gives `r delta_bldg` and `r delta_cont` per flood event, for a total of `r delta_total`. The fiscal calculation below poses the opposite counterfactual---it asks how much less the claims post-1994 homes actually filed cost the program than they would have---so it applies the estimates to the observed post-1994 means instead. The two conversions differ by roughly a third, which is why the paper does not use a single figure for both.

The expected benefit depends on the probability of experiencing a flood. Among manufactured homes in the NFIP data, the baseline claim rate is approximately `r round(get_welf("claim_rate_pooled_pre"), 3)` claims per year, yielding an expected annual damage reduction of `r ann_benefit`. Discounting at 3% over a 20-year lifespan yields an expected present value of roughly `r npv_baseline` in flood damage reduction.

The calculation holds this claim rate fixed across vintages, and Section \ref{appendix-take-up} tests that assumption directly. Claims per policy-year for post-1994 manufactured homes differ from the pre-1994 rate by `r cr_stc_pct` (standard error `r cr_stc_se` in log points), relative to site-built homes of the same vintage and against a pre-1994 rate of `r clmrate_base` claims per 1,000 policy-years. The estimate is not distinguishable from zero, and unlike the other results in that appendix it rests on no imputed quantity, since both claims and policy-years are observed directly. The reform reduced damage per claim without a measurable change in how often a claim occurs, so the whole of the benefit estimated here comes from severity.

The resulting ratio of `r bcr_pct` should be read as a statement about coverage rather than as a verdict. Several factors suggest that these benefits are a lower bound on the total private return. First, and most importantly, the HUD standard targeted wind resilience, not flood protection, but NFIP claims are triggered only by flood events. The flood damage reductions estimated here are therefore only part of the full resilience benefits, and the omitted part is the one the regulation was written to produce. The magnitude required is a stated quantity rather than an open-ended appeal: for the private calculation to break even, the wind channel would have to deliver `r wind_be` in present value per unit, or `r wind_be_mult` times the flood benefit measured here. Whether it does is a question this paper poses and does not answer. Second, damage to buildings and contents represents only one part of losses related to climate disasters, which also include displacement costs, lost income, and other indirect costs. Finally, risk-averse households may value the insurance value of greater protection against climate damages.

However, private benefits may be overstated if households select into NFIP based on their flood risk. Standard adverse selection would imply that insured MH face higher flood exposure than the average MH, so the claim rate of `r claim_rate_fmt` would overstate the hazard a typical MH confronts and the extrapolated benefit would be too high. Conversely, take-up of NFIP coverage is correlated with income, and low-income MH residents---who are less likely to purchase---may occupy lower-quality sites with greater flood exposure, implying the opposite sign of selection [@landry_flood_2011].

Social returns may be yet greater for two reasons. First, the code change caused fiscal spillovers on FEMA via both changes in NFIP payments and FEMA's \emph{ex post} disaster relief, predominantly provided through its Individual Assistance program. Reduced damage to post-1994 manufactured homes reduces these federal outlays, though I do not estimate effects on ex post relief directly.[^fiscal-spillover]

[^fiscal-spillover]: \cite{solomon_optimal_2026} study how changes in insurance take-up (rather than damages) affect relief spending. In principle, FEMA's individual assistance relief does not cover towards insured losses, and they find this borne in the data: an additional 1% of houses that are insured lowers ex post government spending by $175-$203 per house-flood.

# Conclusion

The 1994 HUD wind standard reform raised manufactured home prices by roughly `r price_eff`. Among NFIP-insured claimants, post-1994 manufactured homes experience about `r bldg_dmg_pct` lower building damage and about `r cont_dmg_pct` lower contents damage per claim, which against pre-reform manufactured-home means comes to `r delta_bldg` and `r delta_cont`, or `r delta_total` in total per flood event. Applying the pre-reform claim rate and discounting at 3% over a 20-year lifespan, those per-claim reductions imply roughly `r npv_baseline` in expected present-value flood benefits---about `r bcr_pct` of the price increase. That ratio covers the flood channel alone; the wind channel the standard was written to address would need to supply a further `r wind_be` per unit for the investment to break even on private grounds.

For the 22 million Americans living in manufactured homes---disproportionately low-income, credit-constrained, and underinsured---these findings have policy relevance, with one boundary worth drawing clearly. Because the HUD standard applies at construction, it may provide protection even for households that private insurance markets do not reach; but the estimates in this paper are measured among NFIP-insured claimants, who are likely more selected and more financially connected than the uninsured manufactured-home population the framing highlights. Subject to that caveat, the results suggest that building code reform can generate meaningful disaster-loss reductions, and that the full return may be larger once wind losses, uninsured losses, displacement costs, risk aversion, and fiscal spillovers are accounted for. As climate change intensifies hurricane and flood risk, the returns to mandated adaptation investment in this housing sector are likely growing.

\appendix

# NFIP Take-Up {#appendix-take-up}

The damage estimates in the main text condition on filing a claim and do not speak to whether the HUD code reform affected NFIP take-up. In standard models, self-protection can reduce the private value of insurance when coverage is costly, so the reform could in principle lower voluntary NFIP demand \citep{ehrlich_market_1972}. The sign is not general: it depends on premium loading, mandatory purchase rules, borrowing constraints, and basis risk, and under actuarially fair full insurance a lower loss probability does not by itself imply lower optimal coverage. This appendix examines whether the reform affected the rate at which manufactured homeowners hold NFIP policies and file claims, relative to the stock of homes of that vintage and type -- not just the raw count of policies, which mechanically tracks how many homes of a given vintage exist.

The raw policy count is not interpretable as a take-up rate on its own, since it moves with both take-up and the underlying number of homes of that vintage. An earlier version of this table divided policy counts by county single-family building-permit counts, but that denominator is the wrong housing type (permits for site-built construction, applied to manufactured and site-built rows alike) and undercounts non-randomly: median permit coverage of the site-built stock falls from 0.70 in counties with few manufactured homes to 0.20 in counties with many, exactly where manufactured housing concentrates. I instead construct an imputed stock of homes by county, construction year, and housing type. Levels come from the 2000 Census, which counts a mobile home as a housing unit regardless of titling, so there is no chattel-titling gap; within a Census vintage bin, the annual split uses Survey of Manufactured Housing state-year placements (for manufactured homes) and county-year single-family building permits, falling back to the state permit share where a county reports none (for site-built homes). These annual sources are used only to divide a Census-anchored bin total across years, so their own level bias cancels out of the ratio.

Two features of that division matter for the estimates. First, the Census vintage bins are wider than the construction-year window used here: the earliest bin spans 1980--1989, of which only 1984--1989 is in the window, and the next spans 1990--1994, of which only 1990--1993 is. The annual shares are therefore normalized over every year a bin spans, not over the retained years alone, so a bin contributes only the fraction of its total that the retained years account for. Normalizing over the retained years instead would assign the whole 1980--1989 total to six years and the whole 1990--1994 total to four, inflating the pre-reform denominators by roughly two-thirds and one-third respectively while leaving the 1995--1998 denominators untouched. That inflation falls entirely on the pre-reform side of the treatment split, so it does not cancel: it depresses measured pre-reform take-up, and because the site-built rate is roughly four times the manufactured-home rate, it depresses the comparison group's pre-reform rate by four times as much in levels. Second, construction year 1994 is dropped from the imputation as an ambiguous mix of pre- and post-reform units, given the code's July effective date and production and installation lags. Because that year has no denominator, it is also excluded from the numerators here, so both sides of every rate span the same construction years; the 1994--1995 vintage bin contains only construction year 1995 throughout this appendix. Retaining 1994 in the numerator alone would nearly double that bin's measured rate, since construction year 1994 supplies roughly half of its policy-years.

The within-bin annual split is the weakest link in this construction, so I build a second denominator that does without it. It uses the same Census bin totals, normalized over the same span, but divides each bin equally across the years it covers rather than in proportion to placements and permits. An equal split is a worse description of any bin's true year profile than the annual sources are; it is not offered as an alternative estimate of the stock. Its purpose is to measure how much of a result the annual sources are supplying. Estimates run on the two denominators use identical cells and identical numerators and differ only in the exposure they divide by, so what moves between them is what the imputation contributes. Section \ref{takeup-imputation} reports that comparison.

## Three margins

Tables \ref{tab:take-up} and \ref{tab:take-up-static} report three outcomes that together describe the benefit side's extensive margin:
$$
\underbrace{\frac{\text{claims}}{\text{home}}}_{\text{(2)}} = \underbrace{\frac{\text{policies}}{\text{home}}}_{\text{(1)}} \times \underbrace{\frac{\text{claims}}{\text{policy}}}_{\text{(3)}}.
$$
Column (1) is take-up: who insures. Column (3) is claim frequency conditional on holding a policy, which is the hazard rate the cost-benefit calculation of Section \ref{cost-benefit} applies to the per-claim damage reductions. Column (2) is their product: how often a home of that vintage and type generates an NFIP claim at all. The remaining margin, payment conditional on a claim, is the intensive margin estimated in the main damage tables, which needs no stock denominator.

Each outcome is a count divided by an exposure. I estimate all three as Poisson regressions of the count on the interactions and fixed effects of Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit}, with the log of the exposure entered as an offset: home-years for columns (1) and (2), observed policy-years for column (3). A home-year is one home of that county, construction year, and housing type in one calendar year; a policy-year is one policy term. Each coefficient is therefore a proportional change in the annual rate, and a coefficient of $b$ corresponds to a change of $e^b - 1$. The county $\times$ loss-year fixed effect of Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-benefit} is replaced by a county $\times$ calendar-period fixed effect, and the common vintage and housing-type fixed effects are retained. All columns pool the three policy periods covering 2009--2023.

The identity above holds cell by cell in the data, in consistent annual units. It does not hold among the fitted coefficients: each column is fit against its own exposure, so column (1) plus column (3) need not equal column (2). The three columns describe three margins; they are not a decomposition of one estimate into two others.

Columns (2) and (3) are estimated on fewer cells than column (1). A county and calendar period in which no home of any vintage or type filed a claim contributes no information about claim counts and is dropped from those two columns, while the same cell does carry information about how many homes are insured and is retained in column (1). Restricting column (1) to the claims columns' cells gives `r tk_clm_stc` (standard error `r tk_clm_stc_se`) in place of `r tk_stc`, so the sample difference is not what separates the columns.

## Specification: counts rather than level rates

An earlier version of these tables regressed the rate itself on the same interactions, weighted by the denominator, so that each coefficient was a level difference in annual policies per 1,000 homes. That specification is not identified in its own units. The manufactured-home take-up gap is proportional rather than additive: weighted take-up averages `r tk_rate_low` annual policies per 1,000 homes in the third of counties with the lowest rates and `r tk_rate_high` in the highest third. A single additive housing-type fixed effect cannot fit a gap that differs by a factor of twenty-seven across counties, and the treatment coefficient absorbs the misfit.

Four checks establish that this is what the level coefficient was measuring. The pooled level estimate of the static contrast is `r tk_lvl_stc` annual policies per 1,000 homes (standard error `r tk_lvl_stc_se`). Estimated separately within each third of counties, it is `r tk_lvl_t_low`, `r tk_lvl_t_mid`, and `r tk_lvl_t_high` -- negative in every subsample, though the pooled estimate is positive. Allowing the housing-type and post-1994 fixed effects to differ across the three groups within one regression gives `r tk_lvl_terc`; allowing a separate housing-type effect for each county gives `r tk_lvl_ctymh`; widening the construction bins from two years to five gives `r tk_lvl_bin5`. The sign of the level estimate is a property of the fixed effects and the bin width, not of the data.

The Poisson specification is stable across the same perturbations. The static estimate is `r tk_stc`; a county-specific housing-type effect gives `r tk_ppml_ctymh` and five-year construction bins give `r tk_ppml_bin5`. A proportional specification fits a proportional gap, so there is no misfit for the treatment coefficient to absorb. Poisson also admits cells with no claims without a transformation, and requires no weighting rule, which the level specification did need: a handful of cells have an imputed stock well under one home and would otherwise dominate an unweighted fit.

Standard errors are clustered by state rather than by county. The imputed denominator's within-bin annual allocation rests on a state-year placement series broadcast to every county in the state, and county permit shares within a state move together, so its error is close to one draw per state, vintage, and housing type rather than one per county. Clustering by county credits that error with precision it does not have. The size of the problem is visible directly: regressing the log of the imputed stock on the same interactions and fixed effects -- a quantity containing no policy data at all -- returns a vintage profile whose largest county-clustered $t$-statistic is `r tk_den_max_t`. The county-clustered standard error on column (1)'s static estimate is `r tk_stc_cty_se`, against `r tk_stc_se` clustered by state. Column (3) uses no imputed input and is not exposed to this: its standard error is `r cr_stc_cty_se` clustered by county against `r cr_stc_se` clustered by state.

## Results

No margin shows a measurable change at 1994.

Take-up is flat. The static estimate in column (1) is `r tk_stc` log points (standard error `r tk_stc_se`), or `r tk_stc_pct` on a pre-1994 manufactured-home rate of `r ppl_home_base` annual policies per 1,000 homes. The 95% interval runs from `r tk_ci_lo` to `r tk_ci_hi`, so the estimate is consistent with a substantial fall in take-up and with a substantial rise. This is a null, not a demonstration that the effect is small.

Claim frequency conditional on a policy is also flat. Column (3) is `r cr_stc` log points (standard error `r cr_stc_se`), or `r cr_stc_pct` against a pre-1994 manufactured-home rate of `r clmrate_base` claims per 1,000 policy-years, with a 95% interval from `r cr_ci_lo` to `r cr_ci_hi`. No vintage bin in Table \ref{tab:take-up} is individually significant. This is the object the cost-benefit calculation of Section \ref{cost-benefit} depends on, and it is the one result in this appendix that does not depend on the imputed denominator: column (3) divides claims by policy-years, both observed directly in the policy records. Conditional on holding a policy, the reform did not measurably change how often a manufactured home of a given vintage produces a flood claim, so the whole of the benefit estimated in Section \ref{cost-benefit} comes from severity rather than frequency.

Claims per home in column (2) is `r ch_stc` log points (standard error `r ch_stc_se`), which is the largest of the three but still short of conventional significance. Its two most recent vintage bins are individually significant while its earlier bins are not, a profile discussed below.

Three features of these estimates limit how much weight they can bear, beyond the width of the intervals themselves. First, the vintage profile in Table \ref{tab:take-up} is not a step at 1994. The largest coefficient in column (1) is `r tk_pre_max` (standard error `r tk_pre_max_se`), at the `r tk_pre_max_bin` vintage bin, four years before the reform, and it is larger than any post-1994 bin; the earliest pre-reform bin is `r tk_pre_first` (standard error `r tk_pre_first_se`), of the opposite sign. The profile wanders rather than shifting at the reform. A design that identifies a level break at 1994 does not fit this profile. Second, the estimate depends on the geographic fixed effects, though less than the level version did. Pooled across all counties, manufactured-home take-up moves from `r ppl_mh_pre` to `r ppl_mh_post` annual policies per 1,000 homes across the 1994 boundary while site-built take-up moves from `r ppl_sb_pre` to `r ppl_sb_post`; the same specification without the geographic fixed effects gives `r tk_nogeo` (standard error `r tk_nogeo_se`). Manufactured homes are concentrated in counties whose overall take-up rose least across the vintage boundary, so absorbing that concentration moves the estimate, and both versions are statistically indistinguishable from zero. Third, the denominator of columns (1) and (2) is an imputation while the numerator is not, which the next section takes up.

What the appendix can support is the negative claim it was written to test. Crowding out requires a fall in manufactured-home insurance demand after the reform, and no column shows one. It cannot support a positive claim in either direction: these estimates do not establish that take-up rose, and an earlier version of this appendix that read a positive level coefficient that way was reading the specification rather than the data.

## How much of this is the imputed denominator? {#takeup-imputation}

Table \ref{tab:take-up-robust} re-estimates columns (1) and (2) against the equal-split denominator described above, alongside the imputed one. The numerator, the cells, the fixed effects, and the clustering are identical; only the exposure changes.

The pre-1994 vintage profile does not survive the swap. The largest movement in any pre-1994 bin of column (1) is `r tk_flat_max_gap` log points, which exceeds every coefficient in that part of the profile, and the earliest bin moves from `r tk_pre_first` to `r tk_flat_pre_first`. Coefficients change sign between the two columns. The pre-reform vintage profile is therefore a property of the within-bin annual allocation and carries no information about manufactured homes. The post-1994 bins move much less, because the 1995--1998 Census bin is retained in full and its placement and permit shares are close to uniform within it, so the two denominators nearly coincide there.

The static contrasts move less than the individual pre-1994 bins do, but they still move by an appreciable fraction of their own standard errors: column (1) is `r tk_stc` against the imputed denominator and `r tk_flat_stc` (standard error `r tk_flat_stc_se`) against the equal split, and column (2) is `r ch_stc` against `r ch_flat_stc` (standard error `r ch_flat_stc_se`). Both remain statistically indistinguishable from zero under either denominator, so the conclusion is unchanged, but the point estimates are not pinned down to better than about a tenth of a log point by the data alone. This is the concrete form of the third limitation above, and it is why the vintage profile in columns (1) and (2) is reported as a description of the estimates rather than as evidence about vintages.

## Mandatory purchase

The National Flood Insurance Reform Act of 1994 strengthened enforcement of the mandatory purchase requirement on federally related mortgages in the same year as the building standard, so any movement in take-up across the 1994 boundary could reflect it rather than the standard. Splitting column (1)'s numerator by whether the policy is flagged as a mandatory purchase, holding the denominator and specification fixed, separates the two.

The mandated component does move: its static estimate is `r tk_mand_stc` log points (standard error `r tk_mand_stc_se`), or `r tk_mand_pct`. The non-mandated component is `r tk_nonmand_stc` (standard error `r tk_nonmand_stc_se`). This is what the reform to the purchase requirement would predict, and it is the one clearly signed result in this appendix. It does not, however, account for much of the total, because mandated policies are a small part of the manufactured-home pool: they are `r tk_mand_share` of pre-1994 manufactured-home policy-years. Weighting the mandated component by that share puts its contribution to the overall take-up rate at about `r tk_mand_contrib` log points, against a total of `r tk_stc`. Under a proportional specification the two components do not add to the total, so this is an approximation rather than an exact decomposition.

The flag is reported by the insurer and marks a far smaller share of policy-years than the share of policies in Special Flood Hazard Areas, so it under-records mandate exposure and the split is a lower bound on the mandated part. The reading it supports is that the 1994 purchase-requirement reform is visible in the data where it should be, and is too small a part of the manufactured-home pool to generate a detectable movement in the aggregate take-up rate.
