## Caveat: the stock denominator is a 2000 snapshot, the policy data are not

The imputed home stock is fixed as of the 2000 Census, while the policy periods run from 2009 to 2023 -- 9 to 23 years later. If pre- and post-1994 manufactured homes attrite (are demolished, relocated, or converted) at different rates over that gap, the true denominator drifts away from the Census-fixed one asymmetrically by vintage, and the bias grows with the gap. An earlier version of this table reported the 2009--2013 calendar period separately, as the closest snapshot to 2000 and so the least exposed to this drift; its point estimates were extremely similar to the pooled 2009--2023 estimates, so it was dropped from the table without evidence that attrition is materially distorting them. The American Community Survey's continuously updated housing-vintage tables could in principle bound the drift directly, but cannot substitute for the imputed stock: its year-built categories are decade bins that cannot isolate 1994 even in principle, and its tract-level manufactured-home counts carry very large margins of error. Bounding the 2014--2023 estimates against the decade series is left for future work.

# Water Depth and the Damage Function {#appendix-water-depth}

The building damage estimates condition on filing a claim but not on the severity of the flood that produced it. If post-1994 manufactured homes are flooded to different depths than pre-1994 manufactured homes, or than site-built homes of the same vintage, the estimated damage reduction could reflect that difference in exposure rather than construction quality. This appendix controls for water depth at the time of loss and reports the damage-depth relationship directly.

A claim's recorded water depth is missing more often for manufactured homes than for site-built homes, and the gap widens after 1994: `r wd_miss_mh_pre` of pre-1994 manufactured-home claims and `r wd_miss_mh_post` of post-1994 manufactured-home claims lack a recorded depth, against `r wd_miss_sb_pre` and `r wd_miss_sb_post` for site-built claims of the same vintages. A linear control on water depth would drop every one of these claims, and would drop a growing and unequal share of the two housing types across the reform. Table \ref{tab:water-depth-robustness} instead groups water depth into six bins together with an explicit bin for claims with no recorded depth, so every claim enters every column and the count of observations is identical across columns (1)-(3).

Column (1) reproduces the baseline building-damage estimate of Table \ref{tab:claims-outcomes-static}. Column (2) adds the water-depth bins as controls: the estimate is `r wd_dmg_depth` (SE `r wd_dmg_depth_se`) in log points, against the `r bldg_dmg_lp` (SE `r bldg_dmg_se`) baseline. Column (3) additionally lets the relationship between damage and water depth differ by housing type, so that the treatment estimate is identified only from variation within a depth bin and housing type; it changes little, at `r wd_dmg_depthx` (SE `r wd_dmg_depthx_se`). The building-damage effect is not an artifact of manufactured and site-built homes being flooded to different depths.

Adding the depth bins raises the fit of the regression by about one percentage point. This is not because water depth is constant within a county and loss year, which would leave the depth control nothing to work with and make the stability of the estimate across columns automatic rather than informative. Depth varies substantially within the fixed-effect cells: of the `r wd_n_bins` depth bins, the average claim is in a cell containing `r wd_bins_cell` of them, and only `r wd_one_bin` of claims are in a cell where every claim falls in the same bin. The small change in fit instead reflects the fact that water depth explains little of the variation in damage across individual claims once the county and loss year are held fixed, because damage at the level of a single claim is governed mainly by the size and value of the home. Depth predicts the average level of damage, as Figure \ref{fig:damage-function} shows, without accounting for much of the claim-to-claim spread around that average.

Figure \ref{fig:damage-function} plots the relationship the interaction in column (3) tests for: mean building damage by water-depth bin, separately by housing type, on the same claims as the table (excluding the no-depth bin, which has no position on a depth axis). Damage rises with water depth for both housing types, consistent with deeper flooding causing more damage, but rises more steeply for site-built homes. Manufactured homes experience less additional damage from a given increase in flood depth than site-built homes do, at every depth bin with an appreciable number of claims.

# Price Effects by Home Size {#appendix-section-type}

The fixed-weight index of Equation \eqref{eq:price-index} removes variation in the size mix by valuing a single national basket, but it does not report whether the reform raised the price of single-section and multi-section homes by the same amount. Table \ref{tab:mhs-section-type} answers that question directly. I stack the panel so that each observation is one state, year, and home size, and I estimate the single-coefficient version of Equation \eqref{eq:event-study-cost} with size-specific state and year fixed effects. Identification is therefore within home size, and the size mix cannot enter the estimate for the same reason it cannot enter the index. Observations are weighted by each state's mean 1988--1993 placements (the same base-period weight used throughout Section \ref{empirical-strategy}) times the national base-period share of their size, which reproduces the fixed-weight index where both size-specific prices are published and additionally retains the state-years where only one of the two is published.

Column (1) pools the two sizes and recovers the index estimate. Column (2) interacts the post-1994 treatment indicator with home size. Estimating the same contrast on each size separately, on that size's observations alone and with its own state and year fixed effects, gives identical coefficients, so the interaction is not an artifact of the shared fixed effects. The effect for multi-section homes is roughly twice that for single-section homes. Two readings are consistent with this pattern and the data here do not separate them: compliance may require more material on a larger structure, so that part of the cost scales with size, or multi-section homes may be placed disproportionately in the higher wind zones within treated states, where the binding requirements are stricter.

# Wind-Zone Treatment Intensity by State {#appendix-windzone-intensity}

The binary treatment indicator used in the main cost-side specification (Table \ref{tab:mhs-dose-response}, column 1) codes a state as treated if it contains any Zone II or III county, regardless of how much of the state's manufactured housing stock actually sits in one. This is a coarse proxy: a state can be classified treated on the strength of a single high-wind county while the bulk of its MH stock sits in Zone I. Table \ref{tab:windzone-intensity} reports, for every state with at least one Zone II/III county, the share of its 1980--2000 manufactured-housing stock located in a Zone II/III county, constructed by weighting each county's wind-zone status (24 CFR \S 3280.305, as classified in the eCFR crosswalk) by its manufactured-housing stock from the 2000 Census. Only 3 of the 11 treated states---Florida, Louisiana, and Massachusetts---have more than half of their MH stock in a Zone II/III county; pooling across all treated states, only about 30\% of the 1980--2000 MH stock sits in a Zone II/III county. This intensity measure underlies the continuous-treatment column of Table \ref{tab:mhs-dose-response}.
